newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China diesel price falls, squeezes Sinopec profits.
newsitem.headline: China diesel price falls, squeezes Sinopec profits.

text.p: China's state refiner and wholesaler of oil products, Sinopec, is considering cutting production at some of its refineries because of falling diesel prices, industry sources said on Friday.
Retail diesel prices in China have fallen in many cases below the government set wholesale price at which refiners have to sell, so that Sinopec is unable to cover its production costs.

"Domestic retail prices are falling in line with international benchmark prices but wholesale prices remained unchanged, this is putting a financial strain on the provincial wholesalers and distributers under Sinopec," said a trader with China National Chemical Import and Export Corp (Sinochem) in Hong Kong.
Sinopec pretax profits dropped 2.2 billion yuan to 31.5 billion in 1996.

A Sinochem trader said that in Guandong, southern China, retail diesel prices were just over 1,900 yuan per tonne for diesel. But ex-refinery or wholesale prices, set by the government, were 2,190 yuan per tonne.

The strain has prompted China National Petrochemical Corp (Sinopec) -- which accounts for more than 80 percent of China's refining capacity of 4.3 million barrels per day -- to consider run cuts. The state-company is also lobbying the government to limit import quotas in the third quarter.
China produced 43 million tonnes of diesel in 1996 and imported 4.5 million tonnes.
But imports this year have surged. In the year to the end of April they totalled 2.4 million tonnes, running 77 percent faster than in 1996.
The rise in imports amid falling international prices -- which stand at a 20-month low -- has led to a fall in the retail price and left Sinopec feeling the pinch.
"End-users would rather buy from traders who bring in cheaper imports," said a Sinochem trader in Hong Kong.
But refineries have also been encouraged to produce more diesel because of long term projections of rising demand.
Diesel imports into southern China are now priced at around $168 per tonne (1,394 yuan) on a pre-customs tax basis, compared with more than $175 per tonne a week ago.

A trader in Hong Kong said oil product stocks, made up mostly of diesel, in north-east China were 1.5 million tonnes above normal levels. In the east, stocks were more than 500,000 tonnes above normal.
"This amounts to over two million tonnes of diesel stocks which is equivalent to the total January to June official imports," said the trader, referring to 1996 first-half imports.

A trader in a Chinese oil firm in Singapore said some Sinopec refineries were considering cutting runs to alleviate the stock situation. But they would have to wait for a central decision from Sinopec before runs could be cut.
But senior officials were also meeting in Beijing to decide whether to reduce non-state diesel import quotas for the third quarter.
Only Sinopec, Sinochem and China National United Oil Corp and China International United Petroleum and Chemicals Co Ltd have state endorsement to import.
"We are waiting for the third quarter licences. Normally they would be issued by now, it is just 10 days away before we enter the third quarter," said a Sinochem Hong Kong trader.
